1.pericope_label: In the third year of the reign of king Belshazzar a vision appeared unto me, even unto me Daniel, after that which appeared unto me at the first
debates: When the vision was given
Whom the little horn will turn out to be
Whether the prophet was bodily at Shushan
outliers: Clarke declines the identification of the little horn with Antiochus Epiphanes and applies it instead to the Roman power in general, where Calvin makes the whole vision a preparation for the tyranny of Antiochus

Clarke has the prophet living at Shushan and seeing the river only in vision, while Ellicott, Henry and Calvin all deny that he was bodily there, Calvin asking who could have persuaded a captive of Babylon to travel into enemy Persia
themes: A book that changes language when it changes subject
Four dates offered for one year
A vision given so that later changes will not astonish
A heavenly oracle that no bodily eye could see

3.pericope_label: Then I lifted up mine eyes, and saw, and, behold, there stood before the river a ram which had two horns: and the two horns were high; but one was higher than the other
debates: Why the empire is figured as a ram
Whether the beast is a king or a kingdom
Why the ram does not push eastward
outliers: Calvin knows no reason for the figure of a ram except comparison with the he-goat, and grounds both in the humble origin of the two kingdoms, where Clarke points instead to a ram with unequal horns carved among the ruins of Persepolis
Gill explains the absence of an eastward push by the ram standing in the east and facing west, while Ellicott explains it by conquests already made in that quarter
themes: A horn from a country nobody expected anything from
A shorter horn older than the taller one
A king said to have died in bed by one account and violently by many
A boast of binding the sea with fetters

5.pericope_label: And as I was considering, behold, an he goat came from the west on the face of the whole earth, and touched not the ground: and the goat had a notable horn between his eyes
debates: Why a goat stands for Macedonia
What coming on the face of the whole earth means
How many battles decided the Persian empire
outliers: Calvin takes the phrase about the whole earth of the terror inspired rather than of numbers, since Alexander crossed with only thirty thousand men, where Clarke and Wesley read it of the extent of the conquest

Calvin counts two decisive battles against Darius and treats the speed of the assault as approaching rashness rather than regal bravery, where Clarke names three fields and admires the fire and fury of the charge
themes: A people named after the goats that guided their first king
A leopard given four wings for the same speed
An army worth nothing but empty pomp
A great horn broken at the height of its strength

8.pericope_label: Therefore the he goat waxed very great: and when he was strong, the great horn was broken; and for it came up four notable ones toward the four winds of heaven
debates: Who the four horns are
Who the little horn is
How the phrase out of littleness should be construed
outliers: Clarke declines the identification of the little horn with Antiochus Epiphanes and follows a bishop who makes it the Roman government, where Gill, Wesley, Ellicott and Calvin all take it for Antiochus, Gill setting aside two other readings by name

The lists of the four successor kingdoms do not agree: Clarke names Seleucus, Lysimachus, Ptolemy and Cassander, Wesley substitutes Antipater and Antigonus, and Ellicott offers a division into Thrace, Macedonia, Syria and Egypt or else no division at all
themes: A conqueror broken at the very height of his strength
A dynasty extinguished within fifteen years
A king who called himself the son of a god
A horn described as coming out of littleness

10.pericope_label: And it waxed great, even to the host of heaven; and it cast down some of the host and of the stars to the ground, and stamped upon them
debates: Who the host of heaven are
Who the prince of the host is
When the daily sacrifice was taken away
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch expressly reject the reading that makes the fallen stars the Levites, which is the reading Clarke adopts, and take them for the people of the saints
Gill canvasses the high priest Onias and Judas Maccabeus before preferring God himself, while Keil and Delitzsch and Calvin both refuse the priestly reading outright, Calvin calling it too forced
themes: A horn tall enough to take hold of the stars
A church trodden underfoot and numbered among the stars
A God robbed of the one corner he had chosen
A tyrant skilful only in cunning and flattery

12.pericope_label: And an host was given him against the daily sacrifice by reason of transgression, and it cast down the truth to the ground; and it practised, and prospered
debates: What was given to the little horn
Whether the word means a host or a time
Why the licence was permitted at all
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch reject by name the rendering that makes the word mean a time, which is the rendering Calvin embraces and which Gill reports him as inclining to, holding that the word means only military service and that the same word in the neighbouring verses plainly means host

Clarke refers the giving up of the sacrificial system to a much later ruin, when the measure of iniquity had been filled up, where Ellicott and Wesley keep it to the apostasy of Jews under the persecutions of Antiochus
themes: Apostates handed over to the man they had joined
A tyranny measured out for a fixed term
A worship that may be interrupted but not abolished
A God who might be thought merely unable

13.pericope_label: Then I heard one saint speaking, and another saint said unto that certain saint which spake, How long shall be the vision concerning the daily sacrifice
debates: Who asks and who answers
Whether the two thousand three hundred are days or years
Whether the host trodden down is Israel or the Syrian army
outliers: Calvin insists the number means natural days of twenty-four hours and calls those who make them years or months wretchedly mistaken, where Clarke takes the prophetic day for a year and carries the reckoning past his own century
Ellicott observes that the period falls short of seven years by about two-thirds of a year, and takes this to mean that for the sake of the elect the days of chastisement were shortened
themes: Angels overheard in the middle of a conversation
A questioner too frightened to ask for himself
An answer given to the bystander rather than the asker
A term of chastisement deliberately cut short

15.pericope_label: And it came to pass, when I, even I Daniel, had seen the vision, and sought for the meaning, then, behold, there stood before me as the appearance of a man
debates: Who the man-like appearance is
Why the prophet is addressed as son of man
What the time of the end means
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch deny that the address son of man is meant to humble the prophet, for which they say there was no occasion, and take it to assure him that despite his weakness he was worthy of high revelations, which is the opposite of the sense Wesley gives it

Clarke supposes the man-like appearance to be the Messiah and Ellicott takes it for Gabriel with the voice belonging to his commander, while Calvin and Henry both argue from the giving of orders to angels that the speaker can be Christ alone
themes: A heathen critic said to have found no other way out
A prophet who compared the vision with earlier ones and prayed
A man unable to bear the lustre of what stood before him
A name that means the strength of God taking orders

18.pericope_label: Now as he was speaking with me, I was in a deep sleep on my face toward the ground: but he touched me, and set me upright
debates: What the end of the indignation is
Why the angel raised the prophet up
On what authority an interpreter is to be received
outliers: Calvin objects to carrying the word vision over into this verse from the preceding one, calling that reading harsh and far-fetched, though he grants that all agree as to the matter
Wesley names Antiochus as the instrument of the indignation where Ellicott keeps the wrath general and reads it as belonging to the end of the time of the prophecy
themes: A man face down on the ground and lifted by one touch
Fear set out as the true preparation for obedience
A messenger who takes his confidence from his office
An indignation given an appointed end

20.pericope_label: The ram which thou sawest having two horns are the kings of Media and Persia
debates: Whether the four kingdoms shared the power of the first king
What the name Javan covers
How far the time of the end is bound up with the persecution
outliers: Calvin rejects the rendering that makes the four horns arise from the nations rather than out of the one nation, since it changes the number and loses the point of the angel that the divided kingdoms sprang from a single origin

Keil and Delitzsch hold that the oppression under Antiochus and the return of the Messiah in glory to the final judgment are seen together in one prophetic perspective, a compression none of the other voices attempt here
themes: Two kingdoms coalescing into a single ram
A conqueror dead in the flower of his age
Generals dividing what one man had won
A prophecy offered as proof of its own author

23.pericope_label: And in the latter time of their kingdom, when the transgressors are come to the full, a king of fierce countenance, and understanding dark sentences, shall stand up
debates: Who the king of fierce countenance is
Who the transgressors are
Whose power it is that he does not wield
outliers: Clarke alone takes the king of fierce countenance for the Roman government rather than for Antiochus, on the ground that king is often taken for kingdom or empire, and reads the destruction wonderfully of the taking of Jerusalem
Calvin rejects the reading that makes the prince of princes the high priest, calling it too confined and spiritless, and insists that the king is said to raise himself against God himself
themes: A monarchy already leaning on the power that would swallow it
A priesthood bought and outbid
A king who creeps on by clandestine acts
A power broken by no human hand

26.pericope_label: And the vision of the evening and the morning which was told is true: wherefore shut thou up the vision; for it shall be for many days
debates: Whether the evenings and mornings are days or years
Why a vision given for the people is to be shut up
What the sickness of the prophet shows
outliers: Clarke reckons the two thousand three hundred evenings and mornings as that many years, against Gill and Calvin, who both insist on natural days and on a term of six years and almost a half

Keil and Delitzsch reject the rendering that would make the prophet say he understood the vision not, since on their reading of the command to shut it up the remark that no one understood it would then be superfluous
themes: A term counted out day by day to its close
A treasure guarded by a man nobody believes
A body made sick by what the mind had seen
A prophet back at the palace desk within days
